stem: A 12-year-old boy has had three episodes of meningococcal bacteremia in four years. He has had no other serious infections, his immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte counts are normal, and he has no rash, joint pain or family history of autoimmunity. Complement studies are ordered.
oneliner: 12M + three meningococcal bacteremias + otherwise well + normal immunoglobulins → which complement results?
ask: Which complement result pattern is expected?

options.A: CH50 low, C3 normal, C4 normal
options.B: CH50 low, C3 low, C4 low
options.C: CH50 low, C3 normal, C4 low
options.D: CH50 low, C3 low, C4 normal
options.E: CH50 normal, C3 normal, C4 normal

whyNot.B: Both C3 and C4 consumed means **immune complex disease** (e.g. SLE), with lupus-like features that this boy lacks
whyNot.C: Low C4 with normal C3 is **early classical pathway** loss, typical of hereditary angioedema, with swelling not **recurrent Neisseria**
whyNot.D: Low C3 alone suggests **alternative pathway** problems (factor H/I, nephritic factor), with pyogenic infections and glomerulonephritis
whyNot.E: A normal CH50 means the **whole** pathway works; it cannot explain repeated Neisseria bacteremia

answer: CH50 low (near zero) with normal C3 and C4 (terminal C5-C9 deficiency)
why: Recurrent **Neisseria** bacteremia in a healthy child points to loss of the **membrane attack complex (C5-C9)**. CH50 tests the whole classical pathway through C9, so it is **near zero**, but C3 and C4 are made and consumed normally, so both are **normal**. The MAC is the only defence that kills Neisseria by lysis, so these children get repeated infections.

idea.rule: Terminal complement deficiency = recurrent Neisseria with normal C3 and C4 but absent CH50.
also: Early classical deficiency (C1q, C2, C4): low CH50 with SLE-like disease
C3 deficiency: recurrent pyogenic infections, very low C3
PNH: loss of CD55/CD59 leaves MAC unchecked on RBCs
Eculizumab blocks C5 and raises meningococcal risk, so patients need vaccination

stem: An 18-year-old man has recurrent episodes of nonpitting swelling of the lips and face and crampy abdominal pain lasting about two days. He has no hives or itching, fever, rash or joint pain, and the episodes do not respond to antihistamines. His father had similar episodes. Complement levels are measured during an attack.
oneliner: 18M + recurrent nonpitting facial swelling and abdominal pain + no hives, fever or rash + father similar → which complement pattern?
ask: Which complement pattern is most likely?

options.A: C3 low, C4 low, C2 low
options.B: C3 low, C4 normal, C2 normal
options.C: C3 normal, C4 normal, C2 normal
options.D: C3 normal, C4 normal, C2 low
options.E: C3 normal, C4 low, C2 low

whyNot.A: This is **immune complex disease** (lupus, serum sickness) with consumption of C3; he has no fever, rash or arthritis
whyNot.B: Isolated low C3 suggests **alternative pathway** disease, with infections and glomerulonephritis
whyNot.C: A normal panel fits **histamine-driven** angioedema, which responds to antihistamines; his attacks **do not**
whyNot.D: Isolated **C2 deficiency** causes lupus-like disease and infections, not **recurrent swelling** with a dominant family history

answer: C3 normal, C4 low, C2 low
why: **Nonpitting, non-itchy swelling with abdominal pain** and a family history is **hereditary angioedema** (C1 inhibitor deficiency). Unchecked **C1** keeps cleaving **C4 and C2**, so both are **low**, but **C3** is not consumed and stays **normal**. Immune complex disease lowers **C3 and C4** together.

idea.rule: C1 inhibitor deficiency: low C4 and C2 with normal C3; immune complexes drop C3 and C4 together.
also: Screen HAE with C4 level; confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function
Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency (lymphoma, autoantibody) also lowers C1q
SLE flares: low C3, C4 and raised anti-dsDNA
Terminal complement deficiency: normal C3 and C4, absent CH50

note: Review: levels now measured during an attack, because C2 is often normal between attacks (C4 stays low).

stem: A 3-year-old boy has had eczema since infancy, recurrent otitis media and pneumonia, and bloody stools. His platelet count is low and the platelets are small. His brother died young of an infection.
oneliner: 3M + eczema + recurrent otitis and pneumonia + bloody stools + small low platelets + brother died young → which immunoglobulin pattern?
ask: Which serum immunoglobulin pattern is most likely?

options.A: IgG low, IgA low, IgM low, IgE low
options.B: IgG normal, IgA high, IgM low, IgE high
options.C: IgG low, IgA low, IgM high, IgE low
options.D: IgG normal, IgA absent, IgM normal, IgE normal
options.E: IgG normal, IgA normal, IgM normal, IgE very high

whyNot.A: Pan-low immunoglobulins fit **X-linked agammaglobulinemia**, which has no **eczema or small platelets**
whyNot.C: High IgM with low others fits **hyper-IgM syndrome**, which does not give **eczema or small platelets**
whyNot.D: Isolated **IgA deficiency** is usually mild and has no **platelet** defect
whyNot.E: Isolated high IgE fits **hyper-IgE syndrome**, which does not cause **small, low platelets** or bloody stools

answer: IgM low, IgG normal, IgA and IgE high (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome)
why: **Eczema, small platelets with thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections** in a boy is **Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome** (X-linked, *WAS* gene, actin cytoskeleton defect). The classic pattern is **low IgM, normal IgG, high IgA and IgE**. Patients have T-cell dysfunction and a high risk of lymphoma.

idea.rule: Wiskott-Aldrich: eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, infections; low IgM, high IgA and IgE.
also: WAS is X-linked recessive
Ataxia-telangiectasia: low IgA, ataxia, telangiectasia
Hyper-IgM: high IgM, low IgG, IgA and IgE
Hyper-IgE: high IgE with staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth

stem: A 58-year-old woman has had a low-grade fever, joint pains and pleuritic chest pain for 3 weeks, with a faint rash on her cheeks. She started hydralazine for hypertension 4 months ago. ANA is positive, and her urinalysis and creatinine are normal.
oneliner: 58F + hydralazine for 4 months + arthralgia, pleuritic pain, fever, rash + ANA positive + normal urinalysis → which autoantibody?
ask: Which autoantibody is most characteristic of her condition?

whyNot.A: Specific for **idiopathic SLE** and tracks with nephritis; her **urinalysis is normal**
whyNot.B: Highly specific for **idiopathic SLE**, rare in drug-induced disease
whyNot.C: Typical of **Sjögren** and neonatal lupus; it is not the marker of a **hydralazine**-triggered illness
whyNot.E: Marks **limited systemic sclerosis**, not a drug-triggered illness with **serositis and fever**

why: Hydralazine, procainamide and isoniazid can cause **drug-induced lupus**, which is mild with **arthralgia, serositis and fever**. Kidney and CNS disease are **rare**, and **anti-histone** antibodies are found in nearly all cases. The disease usually clears after stopping the drug.

idea.rule: Drug-induced lupus = anti-histone antibodies, mild, kidney and CNS disease rare, resolves on stopping the drug.
also: Common culprits: hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, TNF-α inhibitors
Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith point to idiopathic SLE
Anti-Ro: subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus heart block
Anti-histone can also appear in some patients with idiopathic SLE

stem: A 19-year-old woman has had an unsteady gait since she began to walk and now uses a wheelchair. Her conjunctivae show dilated small vessels, and she has had frequent sinus and lung infections since childhood.
oneliner: 19F + progressive ataxia since toddlerhood + conjunctival telangiectasias + recurrent sinopulmonary infections → which lab finding?
ask: Which serum level is most likely raised?

whyNot.A: Her recurrent **sinopulmonary infections** fit a **low** IgA, not a high one
whyNot.C: Would point to a **muscle** disease; her problem is cerebellar and vascular
whyNot.D: A marker for **germ-cell and trophoblastic** tumors; nothing in the history suggests either
whyNot.E: A **colorectal** tumor marker; not part of this picture

why: Ataxia, **telangiectasias** and **sinopulmonary infections** make **ataxia-telangiectasia**, caused by an **ATM** mutation that impairs DNA double-strand repair. **AFP is raised**, while **IgA, IgG2 and IgE are low**. Patients are radiosensitive and prone to lymphoma and leukemia.

idea.rule: Ataxia + telangiectasia + sinopulmonary infections = ATM defect: high AFP, low IgA, lymphoid cancers.
also: Low IgA, IgG2 and IgE explain the sinopulmonary infections
Radiosensitivity: avoid unnecessary X-rays and CT
Raised risk of lymphoma and leukemia
Cerebellar atrophy appears on MRI

stem: A 63-year-old man has had fever to 39.2°C for 3 days with a productive cough. A chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation, and sputum Gram stain shows lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci. His white count is 19,800/mm³, and the peripheral smear is reviewed.
oneliner: 63M + 3 days fever, productive cough + lobar consolidation + Gram-positive diplococci + WBC 19,800 → which differential finding?
ask: Which finding on the white cell differential is most likely?

whyNot.B: Seen with **allergy, parasites, drug reactions**; this is an acute bacterial infection
whyNot.C: Typical of **viral illnesses such as EBV**, not a Gram-positive diplococcal pneumonia
whyNot.D: Suggests **chronic infection or recovery**; this illness is only 3 days old
whyNot.E: A marker of **myeloproliferative disease** such as CML, not acute infection

answer: Neutrophilia with a left shift (increased bands)
why: Bacterial infection drives macrophages to release **IL-1, TNF-α and G-CSF**. The marrow releases storage neutrophils, then **immature band forms**, producing **neutrophilic leukocytosis with a left shift**. Toxic granulation and Döhle bodies may also appear.

idea.rule: Acute bacterial infection = neutrophilia with bands (left shift); viral = lymphocytes.
also: Eosinophilia: parasites, allergy, Addison disease, neoplasms (Hodgkin)
Atypical lymphocytosis: EBV and CMV
Leukemoid reaction: high WBC with high LAP score, unlike CML
Neutrophilia from corticosteroids comes from demargination, without bands

stem: A 47-year-old woman has tight skin over her fingers and face, cold-induced finger color changes and heartburn with dysphagia. For 6 months she has had a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion. Fine crackles are heard at both lung bases. Pulmonary function testing is done.
oneliner: 47F + tight skin of fingers and face + Raynaud + dysphagia + dry cough, exertional dyspnea + bibasilar crackles → which PFT pattern?
ask: Which pulmonary function pattern is most likely?

whyNot.A: Seen in **asthma**, not with **basilar crackles** and a fibrosing process
whyNot.B: The **emphysema** pattern; her **basal crackles** point to fibrosis, not airflow obstruction
whyNot.C: Fits **extrapulmonary restriction** such as chest-wall disease; her **crackles** show parenchymal involvement
whyNot.E: Seen with **alveolar hemorrhage** or polycythemia, not fibrosis

answer: Restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO (interstitial fibrosis)
why: **Systemic sclerosis** often causes **interstitial lung fibrosis**. The stiff lung gives a **restrictive pattern** (low FVC and TLC, **normal or high FEV1/FVC**). Thickened alveolar walls reduce diffusion, so **DLCO is low**. Pulmonary arterial hypertension can lower DLCO further.

idea.rule: Parenchymal lung fibrosis = restrictive pattern with low DLCO.
also: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Asbestosis and silicosis
Sarcoidosis (stage IV)
Drug-induced fibrosis: amiodarone, bleomycin, nitrofurantoin
